lesson.menu_title: Making Your Case -- Structuring a Legal Opinion in Spoken English

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Making Your Case
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Paula Teodoro Valdivia | Lesson 3 -- Making Your Case

listenings.text: I am a general counsel, and I ask for maybe forty spoken opinions a month. Here is the shape of a good one. It starts with the answer. Yes, we can sign. No, we cannot sign yet. It never starts with the history of the document. Then it gives me two reasons. Two. Not seven. If you have seven, you have not decided which ones matter, and deciding is what I am paying you for. Then, and only then, it gives me the caveat. There is always a caveat. I am not afraid of the caveat, I am afraid of a lawyer who hides it until the deal is signed. And it ends with the same answer it started with, in the same words. That is the whole structure. Position, two reasons, one caveat, position again. I have watched brilliant lawyers lose a room because they saved the answer for the end, like a detective novel. Nobody in a board meeting wants a detective novel. Give me the ending first.

For years I gave what I thought were careful answers. On the one hand this, on the other hand that. It depends on the circumstances. There are arguments in both directions. All of it was true, and all of it was useless. I remember the exact meeting where I understood. A director listened to me for four minutes, waited, and then asked, very politely, so what would you do. And I did not have an answer, because I had spent four minutes proving that no answer was possible. He did not think I was careful. He thought I was hiding. That is the part nobody tells you. Hedging does not sound cautious to a business person. It sounds like you have not done the work, or like you are protecting yourself instead of them. So now I commit. I say what I would do, in one sentence, and I put the uncertainty where it belongs, in the caveat, with a name and a size. Not everywhere, like fog.

extra_audio.text: In short, my assessment is that we should not sign this version. First, the arbitration clause sends every dispute to a jurisdiction where we have no local counsel. Second, the compliance annex is missing, and therefore we cannot prove due diligence. However, one caveat: none of this is material if the counterparty accepts our standard wording.
